q: Where is the reference datum for Seneca I weight and balance?
a: 78.4 in ahead of the wing leading edge, at the inboard tank's inboard edge
d: At the wing leading edge itself, at the inboard tank's inboard edge
78.4 in ahead of the main wheel centerline, at the fuselage side
At the front face of the nose cone, ahead of the forward baggage door
why: The POH places the datum 78.4 inches forward of the wing leading edge, measured at the inboard edge of the inboard fuel tank. All arms are inches aft of that point, which is why nearly every arm is positive.
drop_reason: duplicate of p2 (p2-043: datum 78.4 in forward of the wing leading edge)

q: What arm does the Seneca loading form use for the pilot and front passenger?
why: The sample loading form lists the pilot and front passenger at 85.5 in aft of datum. 93.6 in is usable fuel, 118.1 in is the center seats, and 78.4 in is the datum-to-leading-edge distance.

q: What arms does the loading form give for the center (middle) seats and the rear seats (seats 5 and 6)?
a: Center seats 118.1 in; rear seats 155.7 in
d: Center seats 155.7 in; rear seats 178.7 in
Center seats 85.5 in; rear seats 118.1 in
Center seats 118.1 in; rear seats 178.7 in
why: Center passengers are at 118.1 in and rear passengers at 155.7 in (the optional jump seat also uses 118.1 in). 178.7 in is the aft baggage compartment, behind the rear seats.

q: What arm is used for usable fuel on the Seneca loading form?
why: Usable fuel (93 gallons maximum on the form) is entered at 93.6 in. The 103.0-in arm belongs to the 5 gallons of unusable fuel, which is already part of licensed empty weight.

q: What are the arms of the forward (nose) and aft baggage compartments?
a: 22.5 in forward and 178.7 in aft
d: 22.5 in forward and 155.7 in aft
-7.8 in forward and 178.7 in aft
43.2 in forward and 178.7 in aft
why: Forward baggage is at 22.5 in and aft baggage at 178.7 in, the two extremes of the loading form. Because the aft compartment has the longest arm, its weight moves the CG aft the most per pound.

q: Where are the Seneca I's two baggage compartments, and how is each one reached?
a: Nose, via a left-side door; aft of seats 5 and 6, via the rear cabin door
d: Nose, via a right-side door; aft of seats 5 and 6, via the rear cabin door
Nose, via a left-side door; in each engine nacelle, via a top hatch
Aft of seats 5 and 6 only, via a separate right-side baggage door
why: The nose compartment (15.3 cu ft) has its own baggage door on the left side. The aft compartment (20 cu ft) behind seats 5 and 6 is reached through the left rear cabin door and can be reached in flight. Each is limited to 100 lb, and the aft placard warns against heavy objects on the hat shelf.

q: At the maximum weight of 4,200 lb, what is the approved CG range?
a: 87.9 to 94.6 in aft of datum
d: 80.7 to 94.6 in aft of datum
82.0 to 94.6 in aft of datum
84.0 to 92.0 in aft of datum
why: The limitations table gives a forward limit of 87.9 in at 4,200 lb and an aft limit of 94.6 in. The 80.7-in and 82.0-in forward limits apply only at 2,780 lb and 3,400 lb.
drop_reason: duplicate of p2 (p2-041: 87.9-in forward limit at 4,200 lb; p2-040: 94.6-in aft limit)

q: What are the Seneca I forward CG limits at 2,780 lb and at 3,400 lb?
a: 80.7 in at 2,780 lb and 82.0 in at 3,400 lb
d: 82.0 in at 2,780 lb and 87.9 in at 3,400 lb
80.7 in at both weights
78.4 in at 2,780 lb and 80.7 in at 3,400 lb
why: Forward limits: 80.7 in at 2,780 lb, 82.0 in at 3,400 lb, 87.9 in at 4,200 lb, varying in a straight line between those points. The aft limit is 94.6 in at all weights.

q: Your loading works out to 4,200 lb with the CG at 87.0 in. Is it within limits?
a: No; it is forward of the 87.9-in forward limit at that weight
d: Yes; it is aft of the 80.7-in forward limit
Yes; only the 94.6-in aft limit applies at gross weight
No; it is aft of the aft limit at that weight
why: The forward limit moves aft as weight increases, reaching 87.9 in at 4,200 lb. A CG of 87.0 in is fine at light weights but forward of the envelope at gross weight; move load aft or reduce weight.

q: At the 4,000-lb maximum landing weight, about where is the Seneca's forward CG limit?
a: About 86.4 in, on a straight line between 82.0 in and 87.9 in
d: 82.0 in, because the 3,400-lb limit applies up to gross
87.9 in, because the gross-weight limit applies above 3,400 lb
About 85.0 in, halfway between the 3,400-lb and 4,200-lb limits
why: The limits vary in a straight line between the tabulated points. 4,000 lb is three-quarters of the way from 3,400 lb (82.0 in) to 4,200 lb (87.9 in): 82.0 + 0.75 x 5.9 = about 86.4 in. 85.0 in is the limit at 3,800 lb.

q: What are the Seneca I's maximum takeoff and maximum landing weights?
a: 4,200 lb takeoff and 4,000 lb landing
d: 4,200 lb for both takeoff and landing
4,000 lb takeoff and 3,800 lb landing
4,500 lb takeoff and 4,200 lb landing
why: The limitations list a maximum weight of 4,200 lb and a maximum landing weight of 4,000 lb; both are marked on the weight vs. CG envelope.
drop_reason: duplicate of p2 (p2-038: 4,200-lb takeoff / 4,000-lb landing); p1-012 is also dropped

q: Which of these weight limits does the Seneca I POH NOT list?
a: A separate maximum ramp (taxi) weight
d: A maximum takeoff weight
A maximum landing weight
A maximum weight for each baggage compartment
why: The POH lists a 4,200-lb maximum (takeoff) weight, a 4,000-lb maximum landing weight and 100 lb per baggage compartment, and a placard requires all weight above 4,000 lb to be fuel, which works as a zero-fuel limit. No ramp weight is given, so the 4,200-lb maximum applies on the ramp too.

q: You take off at exactly 4,200 lb. About how much fuel must you burn before you are at maximum landing weight?
a: About 200 lb, roughly 33 gallons
d: About 100 lb, roughly 17 gallons
None; 4,200 lb is also the landing limit
About 400 lb, roughly 67 gallons
why: Maximum landing weight is 4,000 lb, so 200 lb must be burned. At the POH's 6 lb/gal that is about 33 gallons.

q: Per N56307's 2022 weight and balance report, what is the airplane's corrected empty weight?
why: The 11/18/2022 report weighed N56307 at 3,389.0 lb with its usable fuel aboard, then removed 558 lb of usable fuel to get a corrected empty weight of 2,831.0 lb. 2,625 lb is the POH's approximate standard empty weight; 2,743 lb is the minimum weight on the maneuvering-speed placard.

q: What empty-weight CG does N56307's 2022 weight and balance report show?
a: 85.00 in aft of datum
d: 86.42 in aft of datum
82.00 in aft of datum
80.70 in aft of datum
why: The corrected empty weight of 2,831.0 lb has a moment of 240,641.4 in-lb, so the CG is 85.00 in. 86.42 in is the as-weighed CG with usable fuel aboard; 82.0 in is the basic CG in the POH plotter sample; 80.7 in is the forward limit at 2,780 lb.

q: What useful load does N56307's 2022 weight and balance report list?
why: Useful load is maximum weight minus empty weight: 4,200 - 2,831.0 = 1,369.0 lb. 1,575 lb is the POH's approximate figure for a standard airplane; 1,169 lb (4,000 - 2,831) is the most non-fuel load the 4,000-lb placard allows; 811 lb (4,200 - 3,389) is what remains with full usable fuel.

q: N56307 (2,831.0 lb at 85.00 in) carries 380 lb in front, 250 lb center, 180 lb rear, 60 gal, 50 lb nose and 45 lb aft baggage. Result?
a: 4,096 lb at 91.20 in, within the envelope
d: 3,880 lb at 89.52 in, within the envelope
4,096 lb at 91.20 in, aft of the aft CG limit
4,654 lb at 91.49 in, over maximum takeoff weight
why: Weight: 2,831.0 + 380 + 250 + 180 + 360 (60 gal x 6) + 50 + 45 = 4,096 lb. Moment: 240,641.4 + 32,490 + 29,525 + 28,026 + 33,696 + 1,125 + 8,041.5 = 373,544.9 in-lb, so CG = 91.20 in, between the forward limit (about 87.1 in at 4,096 lb) and the 94.6-in aft limit; without fuel it weighs 3,736 lb, under the 4,000-lb placard limit. 3,880 lb is the POH plotter sample's answer; 4,654 lb comes from wrongly starting at the as-weighed 3,389 lb.

q: N56307 takes off at 4,096 lb, CG within limits, and must return to land 10 minutes later. Which limit is the concern?
a: It will still be over the 4,000-lb maximum landing weight
d: None; a takeoff inside the envelope is good for landing too
The CG will have moved aft of the 94.6-in limit as fuel burned
None; the 4,200-lb maximum weight also applies to landing
why: Takeoff at 4,096 lb is legal, but maximum landing weight is 4,000 lb, so about 96 lb (16 gal) must burn off first. Even at the 19.2-GPH red-line fuel flow on both engines, 10 minutes burns only about 6 gal. The POH says fuel burn does not significantly affect the CG.

q: What does full usable fuel (93 gal) weigh for Seneca loading purposes?
a: 558 lb
d: 588 lb
623 lb
480 lb
why: The loading graph uses 6 lb/gal, so 93 usable gallons weigh 558 lb. 588 lb would be all 98 gallons, but the 5 unusable gallons are already in the empty weight; 623 lb would use Jet-A's 6.7 lb/gal.

q: N56307 (useful load 1,369 lb) is filled with all 93 gal of usable fuel. About how much is left for people and bags?
a: About 811 lb
d: About 1,369 lb
About 1,169 lb
About 781 lb
why: 1,369 - 558 (93 gal x 6 lb/gal) = 811 lb: four 170-lb adults and about 130 lb of bags, not seven people. The POH warns you cannot fill the airplane with seven adults and full fuel. 781 lb wrongly subtracts all 98 gal; the unusable fuel is already in the empty weight. CG must still be checked.
src: OEG App 2 · N56307 W&B report 11/18/2022 · POH 4-1

q: Per the POH, what happens to the Seneca's weight and CG as fuel is burned?
a: CG changes little; it moves down the fuel line and stays in the envelope
d: The CG moves well aft, because the fuel tanks are forward of the CG
The CG moves well forward, often past the forward limit for landing
Nothing changes, because the fuel tanks sit right at the datum
why: The POH states that fuel burn-off and gear movement do not significantly affect the CG; in the plotter sample the point follows the fuel line down and stays in the envelope for landing. Gear retraction changes the moment by only -32 in-lb.

q: In the Seneca POH, what does 'basic weight' include?
a: Empty weight plus unusable fuel and full oil
d: Empty weight plus full usable fuel and oil
Empty weight plus the pilot and full oil
Empty weight only, without unusable fuel or oil
why: Piper defines basic weight as empty weight plus unusable fuel and full oil capacity. On the form, licensed empty weight adds the unusable fuel (5 gal, 30 lb at 103.0 in), and basic weight then adds the oil (16 qt, 30 lb at 49.0 in).

q: How is unusable fuel handled on the Seneca weight and balance form?
a: 5 gal (30 lb) at 103.0 in, added to reach licensed empty weight
d: 5 gal (30 lb) at 93.6 in, entered on the form with the usable fuel
2.5 gal (15 lb) at 103.0 in, ignored as negligible for W&B
16 qt (30 lb) at 49.0 in, added to reach the basic weight
why: The form adds 30 lb of unusable fuel at 103.0 in (moment 3,090) to the as-weighed empty weight to get licensed empty weight. The 2.5-gallon figure is per side; 16 qt at 49.0 in is the oil entry.

q: On the Seneca form, how is useful load (normal category) defined?
a: Gross weight (4,200 lb) minus licensed empty weight
d: Gross weight minus basic weight and full fuel
Landing weight (4,000 lb) minus licensed empty weight
Gross weight minus empty weight and the pilot
why: Useful load = 4,200 lb - licensed empty weight. The POH notes that useful load covers fuel, oil, baggage, cargo and passengers.

q: After new equipment is installed in the Seneca, who must compute the new basic weight and CG, and where is it recorded?
a: The mechanic doing the work, in the aircraft logbook
d: The pilot, on the weight and balance plotter only
Piper, by issuing a revised POH weight page
The owner, at the next annual inspection
why: The POH says the mechanic responsible for the work must compute a new basic weight and CG and enter them in the aircraft logbook. The owner should make sure it is done and update the plotter, and the current values should always be used.

q: When weighing the Seneca per the POH, how is the fuel handled?
a: Defuel, open all drains, then run each engine until it stops
d: Fill all tanks and subtract the usable fuel weight
Drain the tanks only, leaving fuel in the lines and engines
Leave 2.5 gal in each wing as unusable fuel
why: The procedure defuels the airplane, drains through all fuel drains and runs each engine until the undrainable fuel is used and it stops. The 5 gallons of unusable fuel are then added back by calculation.

q: Which is part of the POH's preparation for weighing the Seneca?
a: Seats in the 4th notch aft of forward, flaps up, controls neutral
d: Seats in the full forward position, flaps 25 degrees, controls neutral
Seats full aft, flaps fully down, tow bar removed and stowed
Seats removed, flaps up, all entrance and baggage doors open
why: Front seats go in the fourth notch aft of the forward position, flaps fully up, controls neutral, tow bar in its proper place and all doors closed. The airplane is weighed in a closed building, leveled by blocking the main oleos extended and deflating the nose tire.

q: Per the POH, what can happen if the Seneca's CG is too far forward?
a: It may be difficult to rotate for takeoff or for landing
d: It may rotate early on takeoff and pitch up in the climb
Longitudinal stability drops and spin recovery gets harder
Stall speed rises but handling is otherwise unchanged
why: The POH warns that a forward CG can make it hard to rotate on takeoff or landing. Early rotation, pitch-up, reduced stability and harder spin recovery are the aft-CG problems.

q: Per the POH, what can happen if the Seneca's CG is aft of the approved limit?
a: Early rotation, pitch-up in climb, less stability, harder spin recovery
d: Difficulty rotating for takeoff and a nose-heavy landing flare
A longer takeoff roll from extra tail-down force, but more stability
More longitudinal stability and easier spin recovery as CG moves aft
why: With an aft CG the airplane may rotate prematurely or pitch up in the climb, longitudinal stability is reduced, inadvertent stalls and spins become more likely, and spin recovery gets harder as the CG moves aft.

q: The POH warns of a twin-specific penalty for loading the Seneca heavy. What is it?
a: Less single-engine climb performance, losing a twin's main advantage
d: A higher Vmc because rudder authority is reduced at high weight
A shorter accelerate-stop distance because of better braking traction
A lower stall speed that masks the approach to an engine-out stall
why: The POH says the heavier the airplane, the less single-engine climb it has, so the pilot may lose one of the advantages of twin-engine flight. The single-engine climb chart shows this: about 190 fpm at 4,200 lb vs. roughly 430 fpm at 3,400 lb at sea level.

q: You remove the center seats and strap a 150-lb crate to the cabin floor. How should you check weight and balance?
a: Work weight and moment by hand; the plotter doesn't cover that spot
d: Use the plotter's center-seat slot, since the arm is about the same
Use the plotter's aft baggage slot, since all cargo counts as baggage
No check is needed as long as the total stays under 4,200 lb
why: The POH says the plotter does not cover cargo loaded anywhere other than the seats or baggage compartments, and that the computed method should be used when cargo is carried. You need the crate's actual arm.

q: How is the Seneca weight and balance plotter used?
a: Plot basic weight and CG, then chain a line along a slot for each load
d: Plot each load from the basic point separately and average them
Plot total weight only; the plotter computes CG from fuel
Start at 4,200 lb and subtract each load along its slot
why: Plot the basic weight and CG, put the zero end of a slot on that dot, draw to the load's weight, then start the next slot from the end of that line. The final point gives takeoff weight and CG. Keep the plotter out of the sun; heat can warp it.

q: In the POH plotter sample (basic 2,615 lb at 82.0 in, six occupants, 95 lb of bags, 60 gal of fuel), what is the result?
a: 3,880 lb at 89.52 in, within the envelope
d: 4,096 lb at 91.20 in, within the envelope
3,880 lb at 94.80 in, aft of the limit
4,240 lb at 89.52 in, over maximum weight
why: Loads: 380 lb front, 250 lb middle, 180 lb rear, 50 lb forward and 45 lb aft baggage, and 360 lb of fuel, giving 3,880 lb at 89.52 in, with room for more fuel. 4,096 lb at 91.20 in is the same load on N56307's heavier empty weight (2,831 lb at 85.00 in).

q: Per the POH's CG range and weight instructions, once total weight and total moment are known, what do you do?
a: Divide moment by weight, then plot weight and CG on the envelope
d: Divide weight by moment, then plot moment on the envelope
Subtract the 78.4-in datum offset, then compare with 94.6 in
Multiply moment by 1,000, then compare with the plotter
why: Add the weights and moments (moments from the loading graph or weight x arm), divide total moment by total weight for the CG, and plot that point on the weight vs. CG graph. If it is inside the envelope, the loading is acceptable.

q: Which category and flaps-up load factor limit apply to the Seneca I?
a: Normal category; +3.8 G, no inverted maneuvers approved
d: Utility category; +4.4 G, no inverted maneuvers approved
Normal category; +6.0 G, spins approved
Acrobatic category; +6.0 G and -3.0 G
why: A placard requires operation as a normal category airplane with no acrobatic maneuvers, including spins. The flaps-up positive limit is 3.8 G and no inverted maneuvers are approved; the POH lists no separate flaps-down value.
drop_reason: duplicate of p2 (p2-012: +3.8 G, no inverted maneuvers; p2-015: normal category, no spins)

q: Why does the battery have a negative arm (-7.8 in) in the Seneca equipment list?
a: It is in the nose, forward of the datum
d: It is in the tail cone, aft of the datum
Its weight is subtracted from empty weight
Negative arms mark optional equipment
why: Arms are measured aft of the datum, so anything ahead of it gets a negative arm. The 27-lb, 35-amp-hour battery is in the nose, reached through the forward baggage compartment, at -7.8 in.

q: In the Seneca equipment list, what does an 'X' next to an item mean?
a: It was installed when the airplane left the factory
d: It is required equipment for night and IFR flight
It has since been removed from the airplane
It is inoperative and must be placarded
why: The equipment list notes that items marked 'X' were installed when Piper delivered the airplane. The list gives each item's weight, arm and moment for recomputing empty weight after changes.

q: What does POH Section 8 say about values found by extrapolating beyond the chart limits?
a: Do not use them for flight planning
d: Use them only with an added 25% safety margin
Use them for takeoff but never for landing
They are valid below 8,000 ft density altitude
why: A warning at the start of Section 8 says performance derived by extrapolation beyond the charted limits should not be used for flight planning.

q: Which Seneca performance charts are entered with density altitude instead of pressure altitude and temperature?
a: The climb and cruise charts
d: The takeoff and accelerate-stop charts
The landing distance charts
The stall speed charts
why: The multi-engine climb, single-engine climb, cruise speed and range charts have a density-altitude axis, so use the Altitude Conversion Chart (8-1) first. The takeoff, accelerate-stop and landing charts are entered with temperature (degrees F) and pressure altitude directly.

q: Altitude Conversion Chart example: 25 degrees F at 8,000 ft pressure altitude. What density altitude results, and why?
a: 7,500 ft, because 25 degrees F is colder than standard
d: 8,500 ft, because 25 degrees F is warmer than standard
8,000 ft, because temperature does not change density altitude
10,500 ft, because cold air always raises density altitude
why: The chart's printed example gives 7,500 ft. Standard temperature at 8,000 ft is about 31 degrees F, so colder air makes the density altitude lower than the pressure altitude.

q: What does the flaps-0 takeoff ground run chart (8-2) assume?
a: 80 MPH lift-off, full power before brake release, short-field effort
d: 70 MPH lift-off, full power before brake release, short-field effort
85 MPH lift-off, rolling takeoff, normal effort
90 MPH (Vx) lift-off, full power before brake release
why: Chart 8-2: flap setting 0 degrees, lift-off 80 MPH, full power before brake release, short-field effort, paved level dry runway. 70 MPH is the 25-degree-flap lift-off speed. Your school rotates at 75 MPH for the flaps-0 short-field takeoff; the chart's distances assume the 80-MPH lift-off.

q: Chart 8-2 example: 70 degrees F, 2,000 ft pressure altitude, 3,600 lb, 10 MPH headwind, flaps 0. What is the ground run?
a: 900 ft
d: 615 ft
why: The printed example on the flaps-0 ground run chart gives 900 ft. 1,650 ft is the accelerate-stop answer for the same conditions; 615 ft is the landing ground roll example.

q: You need the shortest ground roll at 4,200 lb on a sea-level standard day with no wind. With 25 degrees of flaps, the ground run is about:
a: About 800 ft
d: About 1,235 ft
About 1,600 ft
About 400 ft
why: Section 1 lists an 800-ft take-off run at 4,200 lb (short-field effort, flaps 25), and chart 8-3 gives the same at sea level standard with no wind. 1,235 ft is the distance over a 50-ft obstacle.
drop_reason: duplicate of p1 (p1-009 covers the 800-ft flaps-25 ground run)

q: Chart 8-3 example: 70 degrees F, 4,000 ft pressure altitude, 3,600 lb, 10 MPH headwind, 25 degrees flaps. What is the ground run?
a: 810 ft
d: 405 ft
why: The printed example on the 25-degree-flap ground run chart gives 810 ft. 1,350 ft is the distance over 50 ft for the same conditions (chart 8-4).

q: What lift-off and 50-ft barrier speeds do the takeoff distance charts assume with 25-degree flaps (8-4) and with flaps 0 (8-5)?
a: Flaps 25: 70 and 80 MPH; flaps 0: 80 and 85 MPH
d: Flaps 25: 80 and 85 MPH; flaps 0: 70 and 80 MPH
Flaps 25: 70 and 90 MPH; flaps 0: 80 and 105 MPH
Flaps 25: 65 and 80 MPH; flaps 0: 85 and 90 MPH
why: Chart 8-4 (flaps 25) assumes a 70-MPH lift-off and 80 MPH at 50 ft; chart 8-5 (flaps 0) assumes an 80-MPH lift-off and 85 MPH at 50 ft, both with full power before brake release and short-field effort. Your school rotates at 75 MPH for the flaps-0 short-field takeoff; the chart's distances assume 80 MPH.

q: What speeds does the flaps-0 takeoff distance over 50 ft chart (8-5) assume?
a: Lift-off 80 MPH; 85 MPH at the 50-ft barrier
d: Lift-off 70 MPH; 80 MPH at the 50-ft barrier
Lift-off 85 MPH; 90 MPH at the 50-ft barrier
Lift-off 80 MPH; 105 MPH at the 50-ft barrier
why: Chart 8-5 assumes flaps 0, full power before brake release, short-field effort, 80 MPH lift-off and 85 MPH at 50 ft, matching the POH's flaps-up short-field technique.
drop_reason: merged into p3-045 (lift-off and barrier speeds of charts 8-4 and 8-5)

q: At 70 degrees F, 4,000 ft PA, 3,600 lb and 10 MPH headwind, how do the takeoff distances over 50 ft compare by flap setting?
a: 1,350 ft with 25 degrees of flaps vs 1,600 ft with flaps up
d: 1,600 ft with 25 degrees of flaps vs 1,350 ft with flaps up
810 ft with 25 degrees of flaps vs 900 ft with flaps up
1,350 ft with either flap setting
why: Both charts use the same example conditions: 1,350 ft with 25-degree flaps (8-4) and 1,600 ft with flaps 0 (8-5). 810 and 900 ft are ground-run examples, and the 900-ft one is at a different altitude.

q: A 50-ft obstacle stands off the end of a sea-level runway. Standard day, 4,200 lb, no wind, 25 degrees of flaps: total distance to clear it?
d: 800 ft
why: Section 1 gives 1,235 ft over a 50-ft barrier at 4,200 lb (short-field effort, flaps 25), which matches chart 8-4 at sea level standard. 800 ft is the ground run alone.
drop_reason: duplicate of p1 (p1-009 covers the 1,235-ft flaps-25 distance over 50 ft)

q: At 4,200 lb, sea level standard, no wind, about what takeoff distance over 50 ft does the flaps-0 chart (8-5) give?
a: About 1,400 ft
d: About 800 ft
About 2,200 ft
About 3,000 ft
why: On chart 8-5 the sea-level line meets the standard-temperature curve at about 1,350 to 1,400 ft, read at the 4,200-lb reference line with no wind. That is a little longer than the 1,235 ft with 25-degree flaps.

q: Why might you choose the longer flaps-up short-field takeoff over the 25-degree-flap technique?
a: It keeps you at or above Vmc and best configured if an engine fails
d: It gives the shortest ground roll and best obstacle clearance
The 25-degree chart is valid only below 3,600 lb
It uses less runway, since flaps add drag on the ground roll
why: The POH calls flaps-up the safest short-field technique when obstacle margins allow, because the airplane is best configured to hold altitude after an engine failure. With 25-degree flaps (70 MPH lift-off) it is momentarily below the 80-MPH Vmc.

q: What does the accelerate-stop chart (8-6) assume?
a: Flaps 0; accelerate to 80 MPH, then stop; full power before brake release
d: Flaps 25; accelerate to 70 MPH, then stop; full power before brake release
Flaps 0; accelerate to 100 MPH, then stop; rolling start
Flaps 0; accelerate to 105 MPH (Vyse), then stop; rolling start
why: Chart 8-6: flap setting 0, accelerate to 80 MPH and then stop, full power before brake release, paved level dry runway. Note that the takeoff engine-failure procedure is written around 100 MPH CAS; a stop from a higher speed needs more runway than this chart shows.

q: Chart 8-6 example: 70 degrees F, 2,000 ft pressure altitude, 3,600 lb, 10 MPH headwind. What accelerate-stop distance does it give?
d: 900 ft
why: The accelerate-stop chart's printed example gives 1,650 ft. Under the same conditions the flaps-0 ground run (chart 8-2) is only 900 ft: accelerating to 80 MPH and then braking to a stop nearly doubles the runway needed.

q: You are planning a sea level standard departure at 4,200 lb with no wind. About what accelerate-stop distance does chart 8-6 give?
a: About 2,000 ft
d: About 1,000 ft
About 3,000 ft
About 4,200 ft
why: On chart 8-6 the sea-level line meets the standard-temperature curve at about 2,000 ft on the 4,200-lb reference line; with no wind that is the answer. Compare about 1,000 ft for the flaps-0 ground run alone.

q: Where do you find the Seneca I's accelerate-go distance?
a: Nowhere; the POH has no accelerate-go chart
d: Chart 8-6, below the accelerate-stop curves
Chart 8-8, the single-engine climb chart
The Section 1 specifications at 4,200 lb
why: Section 8 contains takeoff ground run, takeoff over 50 ft, accelerate-stop, climb, cruise, stall and landing charts, but no accelerate-go data. The POH leaves the continue-or-stop decision to pilot judgment based on loading, density altitude, obstructions, weather and competence; the single-engine climb chart shows what climb to expect.
src: OEG App 2 · POH Sec. 8 index · POH 3-12a

q: You plan to depart a wet grass strip with a slight upslope. How do the Seneca takeoff charts apply?
a: Actual distances will be longer than the charts show
d: The charts are valid; only a tailwind needs correction
Use the 25-degree chart, which already allows for grass
Reduce the chart values by 25%, per the chart note
why: Every takeoff and landing chart assumes a paved, level, dry runway. The POH says chart performance is reduced by uphill gradient, tailwind, and soft, wet, rough or grassy surfaces. The 25% note concerns heavy-duty brakes on landing, not grass.

q: In what order do you work a Seneca takeoff or landing distance chart?
a: Temperature up to pressure altitude, across to weight, then headwind
d: Density altitude up to weight, then across to headwind
Weight up to temperature, across to pressure altitude, then wind
Headwind first, then weight, then temperature and altitude

q: N56307 (2,831.0 lb at 85.00 in): 390 lb in the front seats, 93 gal of fuel, 100 lb in the nose baggage, nothing else. Within limits?

q: Removing the usable fuel moved N56307's CG from 86.42 in (as weighed) to 85.00 in. Why did the CG move forward?

why: Removing weight that sits aft of the CG moves the CG forward; removing weight ahead of it moves the CG aft. The fuel at 93.6 in is aft of 86.42 in, so taking out 558 lb moved the CG forward to 85.00 in. In flight the POH says fuel burn does not significantly affect the CG.
